target_customer: Web developers and startups, especially Ruby on Rails teams, later enterprises
problem: Deploying and scaling a web app meant managing servers; developers wanted to push code and have it run.
business_model: usage-based platform as a service, paid dynos plus add-on marketplace revenue share

competitors.name: Engine Yard
competitors.what: managed Ruby on Rails hosting on cloud infrastructure
competitors.traction_then: Rails hosting leader, sources disagree on start (2006)

competitors.name: Google App Engine
competitors.what: hosted app platform, launched 2008 for Python

technical_complexity.rationale: Building multi-tenant app hosting with git deploys, routing and elastic scaling on EC2 with a tiny team was hard; the platform was rebuilt from scratch in about three months in 2009.

defensibility.rationale: Add-on ecosystem and buildpacks created some lock-in but competitors and AWS could copy the model.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Google App Engine launched 2008, Amazon later added Elastic Beanstalk; Salesforce bought Heroku in Dec 2010 for $212M.

market_need_then: Rails developers wanted simple deploys without sysadmin work; Heroku reported over 25,000 apps in its first two years by April 2009.

branding.name_origin: Blend of heroic and haiku, the haiku half honoring Ruby's Japanese roots, per Heroku's own account; one source disputes the Japanese meaning.

identity.logo: purple rounded square with a stylized mark
identity.mascot_or_character: Samurai Duke variant used for Java support, not a core mascot

branding.brand_signature: Haiku-style naming and playful developer culture, such as haiku-named app names
branding.community_and_virality: Strong developer community; its Samurai Duke Java logo had a trademark story with Oracle.

brand_strength.rationale: Became the default name for easy deployment among startup developers, evidenced by its heavy developer press coverage.

pivots.from: browser-based Ruby editor and app builder
pivots.to: git-push deployment platform as a service
pivots.why: Discovered the hosting platform underneath was the real product (per founder interview coverage)

outcome_analysis: Heroku pivoted from a browser Ruby editor to git-push hosting, launched commercially in April 2009 and grew fast with the Rails and startup community. It raised about $13M and was sold to Salesforce for $212M in cash announced December 2010. Later commentary argues it stagnated under Salesforce, but that is outside this record's sourced timeline.
notes: Total raised about $13M per Xconomy and TechCrunch coverage; round split ($3M 2008 Series A, $10M 2010 Series B) from one search summary, treat amounts as moderately verified. Dealroom lists a $40M valuation, unexplained, ignored. Pivot description from general knowledge and the Xconomy Wiggins interview title, not fetched. Founders' prior employers and education not retrieved, left empty. Competitor Engine Yard start date disputed.
